Preface

The exercises use real numbers from the city you have just arrived in. Newcastle is a good place to learn engineering in: the first railway locomotives, the first house in the world lit by water power, the first practical electric light bulb and the steam turbine that still generates most of the world’s electricity all came from within a few miles of this building. You will be calculating with those things all session.

Every fact is stated in the exercise itself, so you do not need to know the city already — and each one links to somewhere you can read more.

We start with the building the city is named after.

27 minHow Python runs your code

This section involves some introductory reading about how Python works and gives you an idea about the format of this session. Read everything carefully.

1.1 Using this page

Python runs inside this webpage. There is nothing to install. Nothing you type is sent anywhere. Read the table below carefully:

Control Buttons What it does
Run, or Ctrl/Cmd + Enter Runs the code in the box
Reset Puts the original code back
Hint Shows one hint. Press again for the next one
Show a worked solution Shows a full answer

A green tick means a check passed. A red cross means it failed, and the text next to the cross tells you what is wrong.

1.2 Lines that start with #

One piece of Python before the first exercise, because you are about to see it.

Definition. A comment is a note for whoever reads the code. Everything after a # on a line is ignored by Python completely.

# This line does nothing at all.
minutes = 120        # and neither does this part

Python reads the # and skips the rest of that line. A comment is for people, not for the computer, so you can write anything you like in one.

Comments are used all through this worksheet to point at the line you need to change:

seconds = 0          # <- change this line

That arrow is a comment. Deleting it changes nothing and leaving it changes nothing. It is there to tell you where to work.

What a comment should say

A comment should explain why, not what. The code already says what it does.

count = count + 1    # bad:  adds one to count
count = count + 1    # good: this reading was valid, so include it in the average

The first is noise: anybody who can read Python can already see that it adds one. The second says something the code cannot — why it is being added.

Rule. If you need a comment to explain what a line does, a better name will usually do the job instead. A name also cannot drift out of date the way a comment can.

1.3 Your first program

Exercise 1

Run your first program

Let’s write our first Python program straight away. Most of it is written for you. You fill in line 2.

This session is two hours long. The program below works out how many seconds that is.

minutes on line 1 already holds 120. Line 2 must use that name to do the calculation. Write minutes * 60, not the answer.

Change the line marked with an arrow, then press Run.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

One minute is 60 seconds. Use * to multiply minutes by 60.

Write seconds = minutes * 60.

Show a worked solution
minutes = 120
seconds = minutes * 60
print(seconds)

Why seconds = 7200 will not be accepted

7200 is the right number. The check still fails it, on purpose.

There are two checks on that exercise, and they look at different things:

The check What it looks at
the answer is 7200 the value your program ended up with
the answer is calculated the code you wrote to get there

The second one needs to see minutes and a * in your line. Typing the answer in by hand passes the first check and fails the second.

This is not the page being awkward. A program that says seconds = 7200 is a program that only ever works for two hours. Change line 1 to minutes = 90 and it still says 7200, which is now wrong. Written as minutes * 60, it follows along on its own.

Rule. Calculate from the names you already have. Do not type in a number you could work out.

1.4 Background reading

Read the passage below before answering the questions that follow it. It is the only part of this session that is purely reading, and everything after it assumes you have.

Reading

Why Python, and how it runs

Why Python?

You could be taught any language. There are good reasons this course teaches this one.

Your field already uses it. Almost every branch of engineering and science now uses Python for analysis, simulation and data. So learning it lets you read other people’s code, not only write your own.

Somebody has already written the hard part. These are all free, and you will use the first three in Session 3:

Library What it gives you
NumPy fast maths on large amounts of numbers
pandas tables of data you can program, like a spreadsheet
Matplotlib graphs and charts
SciPy statistics, optimisation, signal processing
scikit-learn machine learning

It is easy to read. Python was designed so that a program is easy to read, because a program is read far more often than it is written. You will read your own code in six months, having forgotten all of it.

It connects things together. Instruments, databases, files, web services, programs written in other languages. Much of engineering is joining one system to another. Python is the language most often used for it.

How your code becomes something the computer does

A computer does not understand Python. It understands its own instructions, and they look nothing like the words you type.

So something has to sit in the middle and translate. There are two ways to arrange that, and every programming language picks one.

Translate everything first. A separate program reads your whole file and turns it into a finished, translated program. That takes a moment, and it happens before anything runs. Afterwards you have a new file you can run as many times as you like. Languages that work this way: C, C++, Rust, Fortran. They are called compiled languages.

Translate as you go. A program reads your code and does what it says, working through it as it goes. There is no waiting and no second file. Languages that work this way: Python, JavaScript, R, MATLAB. They are called interpreted languages, and the program doing the work is called an interpreter.

What that means for you

Five differences follow, and they matter for the rest of the course.

Translate first Translate as you go
Waiting before you can run yes no
A second file is made yes no
A mistake in a line you never run found straight away not found at all
Speed fast slower
The same file on Windows, Mac, Linux needs redoing for each works on all of them

You can change your code and run it straight away. Nothing to wait for. This is why Python suits trying an idea out, and why research uses it so heavily.

Some mistakes stay hidden. Python only notices most mistakes when it actually reaches that line. A mistake in a part of your program that never runs is a mistake you never see. This is the most important difference in practice, and you will watch it happen further down this page.

Your file works on any computer. Anyone with Python can run it, unchanged.

Python is slower. Which brings us to the obvious question.

Why slower does not usually matter

At repeated arithmetic, Python is ten to a hundred times slower than a compiled language. That sounds like it should rule it out. It does not, and the reason is worth understanding.

In a real program, the slow part is usually one small piece. That piece runs a very large number of times. And it is not written in Python.

Ask NumPy to add up a million numbers and you write one line. NumPy then does the million additions itself. Its code was translated ahead of time, by the people who wrote it. You say what you want; the library does the repeating.

So: an easy language to write and read on top, fast prepared code underneath. That arrangement is the whole reason scientific Python exists, and Session 3 measures the difference for you.

One last thing about this page

The Python here is the real thing. It is not a simplified version made for teaching. It is the same Python you would install on your own laptop, built to run inside a web browser.

Nothing you type is sent anywhere. There is nowhere to send it. The whole of Python is running on your own machine, in this tab.

Scroll to the end, then answer the questions below.

1.6 Seeing it happen

Reading about this is not the same as watching it. Do it yourself.

Exercise 2

Run it, read the error, then fix it

This program has a mistake on line 3. The name total is never given a value.

Press Run now, without changing anything. It is meant to fail. Read the message it gives you before you read any further down the page.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Put total = 30 on its own line, above print(total). Python has to be given a name before it can use it.

Now look at what it printed, from the top.

Look for What it is telling you
the two lines above the error how far Python got before it stopped
line 3 exactly where it stopped
the last line, starting NameError what it could not do, and which name

Two lines of output appeared before the error. They really ran. Python then reached line 3, went looking for a name called total, found nothing, and stopped there and then.

Now fix it. Add a line that gives total the value 30, before it is printed. Run it again and all three lines will appear.

Show a worked solution
print("step 1")
print("step 2")
total = 30
print(total)

Notice what that told you. Steps 1 and 2 printed before the error. They ran, and their output was real. Python then reached line 3, could not find total, and stopped there.

The mistake was in the file from the very beginning. Python did not see it until it arrived at that line.

Question 4 · predict the output

Now predict one

Same program, one line longer, and back to being broken. Use what the error message just showed you.

Write out everything this program prints — including the error — before you run it.

print("step 1")
print("step 2")
print(total)
print("step 4")

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

Exercise 3

Read the error, then fix it

This program has one mistake: a name is spelled wrong on line 3.

Run it first, without changing anything. Read the error message. It names the line and the word Python could not find.

Then correct the spelling.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Compare line 2 and line 3. The same word is spelled two different ways.

Show a worked solution
price = 12.50
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity
print("Total:", total)

The same thing happened again. Lines 1 and 2 were fine and ran. The mistake sat on line 3 from the start, and Python said nothing about it until it got there. Line 4 never ran at all.

Rule. Python checks a line only when it runs it.

So a line you have never run is a line nobody has ever checked. It may be wrong, and nothing will tell you.

This is why programmers write tests. A test is a small piece of code whose only job is to run the rest of your program on purpose — including the parts ordinary use does not reach. The mistakes then appear now, while you are sitting there looking at the screen, instead of next month in front of somebody else.

The green ticks and red crosses on this page are tests. They are running your code the same way.

20 minShowing your answer with print

A program can work out the right answer and show you nothing at all. print is how you ask to see it.

You have already used it once on the previous page. This lesson covers it properly, because every exercise from here on needs it.

2.1 Nothing appears unless you ask

Definition. print(x) puts the value of x on the screen.

Without it, Python still does the work — it just keeps the answer to itself.

2 + 2            calculates 4, shows you nothing
print(2 + 2)     calculates 4, and shows you 4

This catches people constantly. The program runs, no error appears, and the output area stays empty. The code was correct. Nobody asked to see it.

Exercise 4

Make the answer appear

This program calculates the number of days in 12 weeks. Run it first. Nothing is printed, because nothing asks for it.

Add a print so that the answer appears.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Add a new line at the end: print(days).

Show a worked solution
weeks = 12
days = weeks * 7
print(days)

2.2 Text goes inside quotes

Python treats a word in quotes as text to be printed exactly as written. A word without quotes is a name, and Python will go looking for it.

print("Newcastle")     prints Newcastle
print(Newcastle)       NameError: name 'Newcastle' is not defined

That second error is the one from the last lesson. Python reaches the line, looks for a name called Newcastle, and there isn’t one.

Single quotes and double quotes both work. 'Tyne' and "Tyne" are the same thing. Pick one and stay with it.

Question 5 · predict the output

With quotes and without

The first two lines work. The third one stops the program.

Write down what appears, including the error, before you run it.

city = "Newcastle"

print("city")
print(city)
print(town)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

2.3 Printing several things at once

Put commas between them. print puts one space between each one, and moves to a new line at the end.

print("Total:", 42, "marks")

gives

Total: 42 marks

You did not have to turn 42 into text first. print does that for you, and it will happily mix text and numbers in one line.

Exercise 5

One line, three values

Print exactly this line, using the three variables and commas:

Tyne level 12.4 m

Do not type the numbers into the text — use the variables.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

print(river, "level", level, unit). The word level appears twice for different reasons: once as text in quotes, once as the variable.

Show a worked solution
river = "Tyne"
level = 12.4
unit = "m"

print(river, "level", level, unit)

2.4 Putting values inside a sentence

Commas work, but they get awkward as soon as you want punctuation. An f-string is easier to read.

Definition. An f-string is text with an f before the opening quote. Anything you put inside { } is replaced by its value.

river = "Tyne"
level = 12.4

print(f"The {river} is at {level} m")

gives

The Tyne is at 12.4 m

Compare the two ways of writing the same line. The f-string is one piece of text that reads like the sentence it produces.
commas print("The", river, "is at", level, "m")
f-string print(f"The {river} is at {level} m")

Controlling how a number looks

Put a colon inside the braces to say how you want the number written.

You write You get Meaning
f"{level}" 12.4 as it is
f"{level:.2f}" 12.40 two decimal places
f"{level:.0f}" 12 no decimal places
f"{1234567:,}" 1,234,567 commas between thousands

.2f is the one you will use most. Measurements and money are almost always written to a fixed number of decimal places, whatever the calculation produced.

Exercise 6

Write it as a sentence

Produce exactly this line:

Tyne: 12.40 m on 3 days

The level must show two decimal places, and every value must come from a variable.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Start with print(f"..."), then put each variable name inside { }.

{level} on its own gives 12.4. To get 12.40 you need {level:.2f}.

Show a worked solution
river = "Tyne"
level = 12.4
days = 3

print(f"{river}: {level:.2f} m on {days} days")

Why the `f` matters

Leave the f off and nothing is replaced. Python prints the braces themselves:

print("The {river} is at {level} m")

gives

The {river} is at {level} m

No error, no warning, and a line of output that is obviously wrong the moment you look at it. If your braces are showing, you forgot the f.

Exercise 7

A journey on the Metro

The Tyne and Wear Metro runs from the coast into the city. Work out the journey time and print it as a sentence.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

total_minutes = stops * minutes_per_stop.

The line to print is f"{line} line: {stops} stops, {total_minutes:.1f} minutes".

Show a worked solution

The Metro opened in 1980 and was Britain’s first light rapid transit system — 60 stations over 77.5 km, and the first railway in the country to be built in metric units. Read more: Tyne and Wear Metro.

Exercise 8

Three broken lines

Each of these three lines is meant to print something sensible. Each has a different fault:

  1. the quotes are missing, so Python looks for a name that does not exist
  2. the f is missing, so the braces are printed instead of the values
  3. nothing is printed at all, because there is no print

Fix all three. The output should be exactly:

Newcastle
The Tyne is at 12.4 m
84
Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Line 1: either put Newcastle in quotes, or print the variable city instead. Both give the same output.

Line 2 needs an f before the opening quote.

Line 3 needs print(...) around it.

Show a worked solution

Exercise 9

The first room in the world lit by electric light

On 3 February 1879, in a hall on Westgate Road about ten minutes from here, Joseph Swan showed a working electric light bulb to an audience of over 700 people. On 20 October 1880, in the same building, he lit the room itself — the first public room in the world lit by electric light.

The building is the Literary and Philosophical Society, and it is still open, and still a library. You can walk in.

Print one line for each event, in exactly this form:

1879: Swan demonstrates the lamp to 700 people
1880: the Lit & Phil becomes the first public room lit by electric light

Use the variables. Do not type the years into the text.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Each line is print(f"...") with { } around the variable names.

The first line needs two values in it: {demonstration} and {audience}.

Show a worked solution
demonstration = 1879
lighting = 1880
audience = 700

print(f"{demonstration}: Swan demonstrates the lamp to {audience} people")
print(f"{lighting}: the Lit & Phil becomes the first public room lit by electric light")

Swan patented his carbon-filament lamp in 1880, the year before Edison’s company began selling theirs; the two eventually merged their British businesses. Read more: Joseph Swan.

Rule. If you expected output and got none, look for a missing print. If you got { } in your output, look for a missing f. If you got a NameError, look for missing quotes. Those three account for most of the printing mistakes people make in their first week.

22 minArithmetic and expressions

3.1 Operators

Python does arithmetic with the symbols you already know, and two you may not.

Operator Meaning Example Result
+ add 7 + 2 9
- subtract 7 - 2 5
* multiply 7 * 2 14
/ divide 7 / 2 3.5
// divide, and throw away the remainder 7 // 2 3
% the remainder only 7 % 2 1
** raise to a power 7 ** 2 49

The last three are worth learning properly. // and % are the two halves of one operation: 7 // 2 is how many whole 2s fit into 7, and 7 % 2 is what is left over.

Definition. An expression is anything Python can calculate a value from. 7, 7 + 2, and price * quantity are all expressions.

3.2 Two kinds of number

Python has two number types.

  • An integer is a whole number: 3, -40, 1000000.
  • A float is a number with a decimal point: 3.5, -0.001, 2.0.

Most operators give you an integer when both inputs are integers.

/ is the exception. It always produces a float, even when the division is exact.

6 / 3       gives 2.0, not 2
6 // 3      gives 2

Question 6 · predict the output

Three kinds of division

Predict all four lines before you run this.

print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(-7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

3.3 Order of operations

Python follows the usual mathematical order:

  1. brackets
  2. **
  3. *, /, //, %
  4. +, -

Operators at the same level are applied left to right.

Rule. When the order is not obvious to a reader, add brackets. They cost nothing and they remove all doubt.

2 + 3 * 4        gives 14, not 20
(2 + 3) * 4      gives 20

Exercise 10

Split a duration

You walk from campus to the Quayside and back, and it takes 3,725 seconds. Convert that into hours, minutes and seconds.

Use // to get each whole unit, and % to get what remains.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

There are 3600 seconds in an hour. total_seconds // 3600 gives the whole hours.

total_seconds % 3600 gives the seconds that are left over after the whole hours have been removed.

Then repeat the same two steps on remaining, using 60 instead of 3600.

Show a worked solution
total_seconds = 3725

hours = total_seconds // 3600
remaining = total_seconds % 3600
minutes = remaining // 60
seconds = remaining % 60

print(f"{hours}h {minutes}m {seconds}s")

3.4 Built-in functions for numbers

Python has some built-in functions for numbers.

Function Meaning
round(x) round to the nearest whole number
abs(x) the size of a number, ignoring its sign
max(a, b, ...), min(a, b, ...) the largest, the smallest of the values given

round has one behaviour that catches almost everybody. It is easier to see it than to be told about it.

Exercise 11

Change the number, and the surprise goes away

Press Run without changing anything.

You would expect 1, 2, 3, 4 — that is what you were taught at school. What you actually get is 0, 2, 2, 4. Two of the four are not what you expect.

That only happens at exactly a half. Anything above a half rounds up, normally, every time.

Change every .5 to .6 and run it again. All four lines now round up.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Change 0.5 to 0.6, and do the same to the other three lines.

Show a worked solution
print(round(0.6))
print(round(1.6))
print(round(2.6))
print(round(3.6))

So round is only strange at exactly a half. Everywhere else it does what you expect.

3.5 What round does at a half

Python’s round does not round halves upwards. It rounds to the nearest even number.

You write You get Why
round(0.5) 0 0 is even, 1 is not
round(1.5) 2 2 is even
round(2.5) 2 2 is even, 3 is not
round(3.5) 4 4 is even
round(0.6) 1 not a half, so the ordinary rule applies

This is deliberate. Always rounding halves upwards adds a small bias to every total, because you would round up more often than you round down. Rounding to even cancels that out over many values. Most scientific software does the same.

Question 7

Check yourself

What does round(4.5) give?

What a coding assistant is, and where it will let you down

Throughout this course you will see the phrase a coding assistant. It means an AI tool that writes code when you describe what you want — ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and the rest. Most of you already use one. This course assumes you will.

Some blocks in these worksheets are labelled the machine wrote this. The code in them was produced by such a tool, and your job is to find what is wrong with it and fix it. That is a skill you will need constantly, because reading code somebody else wrote — with suspicion — is most of what programming is now.

Rounding is a good example of where they fail. Ask one to “round halves upwards” and it will very likely hand you round(x), because rounding halves upwards is what most people are taught and what most other languages do. Python is the unusual one here, and the assistant gives the ordinary answer.

Rule. An assistant is most likely to be wrong exactly where the language does something unusual — and those are the places where being wrong costs you most.

Exercise 12

Round money the way a till would

A shop till must round to the nearest penny, and at exactly half a penny it must always round up — a customer should never lose money to a rounding rule.

round cannot do that, for the reason you have just seen: at exactly a half it goes to the nearest even number instead. round(2.675, 2) gives 2.67, which is a penny short.

So build it yourself, out of two pieces.

int(x) throws the decimal part away. It does not round at all. int(3.9) is 3, and so is int(3.2). (int is properly introduced in the next lesson; here you only need what it does to a number with a decimal part.)

Adding 0.5 before you do that turns it into rounding halves up. 2.5 + 0.5 is 3.0, and int(3.0) is 3. Anything below the half still falls back down: 2.4 + 0.5 is 2.9, and int(2.9) is 2.

Pennies need one extra step at each end, because int can only give you a whole number:

  1. multiply by 100, so that pennies become whole numbers
  2. add 0.5
  3. take int of the result
  4. divide by 100, to get back to pounds

Use int to do the converting. Do not use round anywhere in your answer — the checks look at your code as well as your answer, and will refuse it.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

price * 100 is 267.5. Add 0.5 to get 268.0, then int() gives 268.

The whole first line is pennies = int(price * 100 + 0.5). Note where the brackets close: the + 0.5 happens inside int(), not after it.

Then pounds = pennies / 100 turns pennies back into pounds.

Show a worked solution
price = 2.675

pennies = int(price * 100 + 0.5)
pounds = pennies / 100

print(pounds)

Exercise 14

Work out a bill

VAT is a sales tax added to most things you buy in the UK. The standard rate is 20%. A shop works out the price of the goods first — the subtotal — then adds 20% of that as VAT, and the customer pays the two together.

A shop sells cable at £3.75 per metre. A customer buys 12 metres.

Calculate the subtotal, the VAT, and the total the customer pays.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

subtotal = price_per_metre * metres.

VAT is the subtotal times the rate. The total is the subtotal plus the VAT.

Show a worked solution
price_per_metre = 3.75
metres = 12
vat_rate = 0.20

subtotal = price_per_metre * metres
vat = subtotal * vat_rate
total = subtotal + vat

print(f"Subtotal: {subtotal}")
print(f"VAT:      {vat}")
print(f"Total:    {total}")

Put the brackets in the right place

The three lines below should each produce the value in the comment. Each one is missing brackets.

Add brackets so that all three are correct. Do not change any of the numbers.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Python does * and / before + and -. Brackets go around the part you want done first.

Show a worked solution

Exercise 16

The tilting bridge

The Gateshead Millennium Bridge is the only tilting bridge of its kind. The whole structure rotates to let ships pass beneath it.

Every number you need is already in the starter code. Work out how fast it turns, and convert its mass into tonnes.

The bridge tilts a total of 40 degrees over a period of 4 minutes.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Four minutes is 4 * 60 seconds.

A rate is one quantity divided by another: degrees divided by seconds.

Show a worked solution
degrees = 40
minutes = 4
mass_kg = 850000
kg_per_tonne = 1000

seconds = minutes * 60
degrees_per_second = degrees / seconds
tonnes = mass_kg / kg_per_tonne

print(f"{degrees_per_second} degrees per second")
print(f"{tonnes} tonnes of bridge")

The bridge opened in 2001 and was the first tilting bridge ever built. It takes about four minutes to rotate, and costs roughly £4 in electricity each time. Read more: Gateshead Millennium Bridge.

Exercise 17

Climbing Grey’s Monument

24 minValues and types

4.1 Three types to start with

Definition. A value is a piece of data. Every value has a type, which decides what you can do with it.

Type Written Example
int a whole number 42
float a number with a decimal point 42.0
str text in quotes, a string "42"

42, 42.0 and "42" look similar. They are three different values of three different types, and they behave differently.

The function type() tells you which one you have.

type(42)        gives <class 'int'>
type(42.0)      gives <class 'float'>
type("42")      gives <class 'str'>

Rule. Quotes make a string. "42" is text that happens to contain digits. Python will not do arithmetic with it.

4.2 What the operators do to strings

+ and * work on strings, but they do not mean what they mean for numbers.

Expression Result Name
"ab" + "cd" "abcd" concatenation
"ab" * 3 "ababab" repetition
"ab" - "b" an error there is no such operation
"2" + 2 an error Python will not guess

That last row matters. Some languages would quietly turn 2 into "2" and give you "22". Python refuses, because guessing is how silent bugs are made.

Definition. len(x) gives the length of a string — how many characters are in it. len("Tyne") is 4, and len("") is 0. It counts spaces too, so len("a b") is 3.

Putting a new line inside a string

A string is written on one line of your program. So how do you put a value in it that spans two lines?

You cannot press Enter in the middle of the quotes — that is a syntax error. Instead you write two characters, a backslash and an n:

"first\nsecond"

Definition. \n is the newline character. Python reads the backslash as “the next character means something special”, so \n is not a backslash followed by an n. It is one character, meaning start a new line here.

print("first\nsecond")

prints

first
second

You have been using it without knowing. Every print ends with a newline — that is why each print starts a fresh line — and that is the end="\n" you will meet in a later lesson.

A backslash marks the start of a few of these. You only need the first one in this course.

You write You get
\n a new line
\t a tab
\" a double quote, inside a double-quoted string
\\ one backslash

Numbers, or text that looks like numbers?

This exercise asks for four things.

The first two use type(), which reports what kind of value something is. The answer is itself a value, so you can store it in a variable: number_type = type(42).

The last two show the difference the quotes make. joined puts two strings together — "42" + "42" gives the six-character string "4242", because + on strings joins them end to end. added does arithmetic on two numbers — 42 + 42 gives 84.

Same operator, same digits on the screen, two completely different results. The quotes are what decides which one happens.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

type(42) is already the answer for the first line. You do not need to write the word int yourself.

"42" + "42" joins two strings. 42 + 42 adds two numbers. The quotes decide which happens.

Show a worked solution
number_type = type(42)
text_type = type("42")
joined = "42" + "42"
added = 42 + 42

print(number_type, text_type)
print(joined, added)

4.3 Converting between types

Three functions convert a value from one type to another.

Function Turns it into Example
int(x) an integer int("42") gives 42
float(x) a float float("3.5") gives 3.5
str(x) a string str(42) gives "42"

int() on a float throws the decimal part away. It does not round. int(3.9) gives 3.

4.4 Floats are not exact

Before the next question, run this in your head and then look at what Python really does.

print(0.1 + 0.2)

You would expect 0.3. Python prints:

0.30000000000000004

That is not a bug, and it is not Python being careless. A float is stored in binary, using a fixed number of bits.

Think about writing one third as a decimal: 0.3333…, and you have to stop somewhere, so what you write down is slightly wrong. Binary has the same problem with different numbers. 0.1 cannot be written exactly in binary, however many bits you use. A tiny error is stored instead, and adding two of them makes the error big enough to see.

Every language that uses these floats behaves the same way. C, Java and JavaScript all print those same digits.

With that in mind:

Question 9 · predict the output

Two numbers that should be equal

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

Exercise 20

Compare floats safely

total should be 0.3, but floating-point arithmetic makes it slightly larger.

Set exactly_equal using ==, and close_enough using the rule above. Use a tolerance of 0.0001.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

total == target is already True or False. Assign it directly.

abs(total - target) is the size of the difference, ignoring its sign. Compare that with 0.0001 using <.

Show a worked solution
total = 0.1 + 0.2
target = 0.3

exactly_equal = total == target
close_enough = abs(total - target) < 0.0001

print("exactly equal:", exactly_equal)
print("close enough :", close_enough)

Where this bites in real work

This is not a curiosity. Money is the classic case. Adding 0.10 to a running total ten times does not give exactly 1.00, so a shop’s till can disagree with its own receipts by a penny.

The usual fix is to store money as a whole number of pence, so every value is an integer and the arithmetic is exact. Python also has a decimal module for cases where you need exact decimal fractions.

22 minVariables

5.1 Assignment

Definition. An assignment statement gives a name to a value.

credits = 20
module = "EEE8165"
pass_mark = 50.0

The name goes on the left, the value on the right. Python calculates the right side first, then attaches the name to the result.

A useful way to picture this is a state diagram: a list of the names that exist, and what each one refers to.

5.2 Names can be reassigned

A name is not fixed to one value. Assigning to it again moves it.

count = 1
count = 2

After those two lines, count is 2. There is no record of the 1.

This is why the order of statements matters, and why reading a program from the top is the only reliable way to know what a name holds.

Question 11 · predict the output

What is printed?

Read the program from the top, one line at a time.

a = 5
b = a
a = 10
print(a)
print(b)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

5.3 Rules for names

Python requires:

  • letters, digits and underscores only
  • it may not start with a digit
  • it may not be a keyword

Keywords are the words Python reserves for itself. There are 35 of them, including if, for, def, class, return, import, True, False and None.

Breaking any of these rules is a syntax error, and the program will not run at all.

Illegal Why
2nd_mark = 60 starts with a digit
pass mark = 50 contains a space
class = "EEE8165" class is a keyword

Beyond the rules, there is a convention. Python names use lower_case_with_underscores. Names should say what the value is.

Rule. n is a bad name. student_count is a good name. You will read your own code far more often than you write it.

Question 12

Which of these are legal names?

Select every name Python will accept. There is more than one.

5.4 An update uses the old value

This line appears in almost every program you will ever write:

total = total + 1

It is not a mathematical equation, and it is not a contradiction. Python calculates the right side first, using the current value of total, then moves the name to the result.

There is a shorter way to write the same thing:

total += 1        the same as  total = total + 1
count *= 2        the same as  count = count * 2

Rule. A name must already exist before you can update it. total = total + 1 fails with a NameError if total was never assigned. This is why counters are always set to 0 before the loop that fills them.

16 minStatements and printing options

6.1 Expressions and statements

Two words that are often confused, and the difference explains a common error.

Definition. An expression produces a value. 2 + 2, "ab" * 3 and type(42) are expressions.

Definition. A statement performs an action. total = 5 is a statement: it changes what exists, but it does not produce a value.

This is why you cannot write x = (total = 5). Assignment is a statement, so there is no value for x to receive.

Line Kind
2 + 2 expression
total = 2 + 2 statement, containing an expression
print(total) expression, whose value is None
import math statement

6.2 More control over printing

You already know print and f-strings from lesson 2. Three more options are worth knowing, and one point about print itself.

print converts types for you. print("Total:", 42, "marks") works even though 42 is a number and the rest is text. This is the one place Python converts types without being asked. Anywhere else, mixing them is an error you will meet in the next lesson.

sep and end change how print joins and finishes.

Option Effect Example Output
sep= what goes between the values print("a", "b", sep="-") a-b
end= what goes after the last one print("a", end="") a, no new line

By default sep is a single space and end is a new line. That is why print("Total:", 42) has a space in it and why each print starts a new line.

Alignment pads a value to a fixed width, which is how you line up a table. Inside an f-string, after the colon:

You write Meaning
{name:<12} pad on the right, so the text starts at the left of 12 spaces
{name:>12} pad on the left, so the text ends at the right of 12 spaces
{name:^12} centre it in 12 spaces

← Variables6 of 13Three kinds of error →

25 minThree kinds of error

Programs go wrong in exactly three ways. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you where to start, so this is the most useful classification in the course.

Kind When Python notices What you see
Syntax error before anything runs nothing runs at all
Runtime error when it reaches the bad line earlier lines already ran
Semantic error never it runs, and gives a wrong answer

7.1 Syntax errors

The text is not valid Python, so Python cannot make sense of the file at all. Nothing runs, not even line 1.

print("hello"          missing closing bracket
print(3 +              nothing to add to
total = = 4            two equals signs

These are the easiest to fix. Python refuses immediately and points at the line.

7.2 Runtime errors

The text is valid, but something goes wrong while it runs. You met one in Lesson 1: a name that does not exist.

Error Cause
NameError a name that was never assigned, or is misspelled
TypeError an operation the types do not support, such as "2" + 2
ZeroDivisionError dividing by zero
ValueError a value the operation cannot work with, such as int("abc")

TypeError and ValueError are easy to confuse. The difference is what kind of thing you gave Python against what was in it.

  • int("12") works. int is happy to be handed text — turning text into a number is its job.
  • int("abc") fails with a ValueError. The kind of thing is still right, a piece of text, but there is no number written in it. The value is the problem.
  • "age: " + 30 fails with a TypeError. Here it is not about which number it is: you cannot add a number to text at all. The kind of thing is the problem.

The important property: everything before the failing line has already run. That is what makes an interpreted language different, and it is why the output you see before the error is useful evidence.

Exercise 29

Three short programs are described below. Set each variable to the name of the error Python reports, as a string.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

int("twelve") is text, which int will accept — but there is no number written in it, so the value is the problem. That is a ValueError.

Show a worked solution

# Program B:  total = 10 / 0
# Program C:  print("age: " + 30)

error_a = "ValueError"
error_b = "ZeroDivisionError"
error_c = "TypeError"

print(error_a, error_b, error_c)

7.3 Semantic errors

The hardest kind. The program runs, produces no error, and the answer is wrong.

Python cannot help you here. It did exactly what you asked. The mistake is that what you asked for is not what you meant.

The only defence is checking the answer against something you already know.

Exercise 30 · check the AI's answer

An AI model wrote this. It runs. Every answer is wrong.

An assistant was asked for “a program to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit”. It produced the code below.

The correct formula is: multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32.

Run the code. Water freezes at 0 °C, which is 32 °F. Water boils at 100 °C, which is 212 °F. Compare those with what the program prints.

Then fix the formula.

Written by an AI model · a general-purpose coding assistant · 2026-08-21

celsius_freezing = 0
celsius_boiling = 100

fahrenheit_freezing = celsius_freezing * (9 / 5 + 32)
fahrenheit_boiling = celsius_boiling * (9 / 5 + 32)

print("freezing:", fahrenheit_freezing)
print("boiling :", fahrenheit_boiling)

Nobody has checked this. That is your job.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Run it first. Freezing should print 32.0. What does it print?

The brackets are in the wrong place. + 32 is inside them, so 32 is being multiplied by the temperature instead of added at the end.

Show a worked solution
celsius_freezing = 0
celsius_boiling = 100

fahrenheit_freezing = celsius_freezing * 9 / 5 + 32
fahrenheit_boiling = celsius_boiling * 9 / 5 + 32

print("freezing:", fahrenheit_freezing)
print("boiling :", fahrenheit_boiling)

Notice how this bug was found. Not by reading the code, and not by Python. It was found because 0 °C is 32 °F is a fact you already knew, and the program disagreed with it.

Rule. Before you run a program, decide what the answer should be for one input you can check by hand. A program that gets a known case wrong is wrong, however convincing the code looks.

7.4 How to debug

When something goes wrong, work in this order.

  1. Read the error message. It names the error type and the line. Beginners skip this; it usually contains the answer.
  2. Check what actually ran. Output printed before the error tells you how far Python got.
  3. Print the values. Add print calls to see what each name holds just before the failure.
  4. Reduce the program. Remove lines until the error goes away. The last line you removed contains the problem.
  5. Check one case by hand. For semantic errors this is the only method that works.

← Statements and printing options7 of 13Functions →

28 minFunctions

8.1 Defining a function

Definition. A function is a named block of code that you can run whenever you want, as many times as you want.

def greet():
    print("Hello")

Four things to notice:

  1. def starts the definition.
  2. greet is the name. The rules are the same as for variable names.
  3. The brackets hold the parameters. This one has none.
  4. The colon ends the header, and the indented lines below are the body.

Python uses indentation to decide what is inside the function. Four spaces is the convention. Every line of the body must be indented by the same amount.

Defining a function does not run it. To run it, call it:

greet()

8.2 Parameters

A parameter is a name that receives a value when the function is called.

def greet(name):
    print("Hello", name)

greet("Ada")
greet("Grace")

Definition. The name in the definition, name, is a parameter. The value supplied at the call, "Ada", is an argument.

A function can take several parameters, separated by commas. The arguments are matched to them in order.

8.3 Returning a value

A function that prints shows you something. A function that returns gives a value back, which you can store and use.

def double(x):
    return x * 2

result = double(21)

result now holds 42.

This is the difference that catches every beginner:

Shows the value Gives the value back
print(x) yes no
return x no yes

return also ends the function immediately. Any lines after it do not run.

Rule. If you want to use a function’s answer, it must return. A function that only prints gives back None, and None is almost never what you wanted.

    return width * height

An AI model wrote this. The first line of output is wrong.

An assistant was asked for “a function that calculates a student’s average mark and lets me use the result”. It produced the code below.

Run it. The first line prints Average: None.

The function displays the average, but it does not give it back. So result is None, and the total on the second line is wrong too.

Fix the function so it returns the average. Keep the two print calls at the bottom exactly as they are.

Written by an AI model · a general-purpose coding assistant · 2026-08-21

    mean = (a + b + c) / 3
    print(mean)

result = average(58, 71, 63)

print("Average:", result)
print("Scaled to 200:", result * 2)

Nobody has checked this. That is your job.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Run it unchanged. result is None, and the second print then fails.

Change print(mean) to return mean.

Show a worked solution
def average(a, b, c):
    mean = (a + b + c) / 3
    return mean

result = average(58, 71, 63)

print("Average:", result)
print("Scaled to 200:", result * 2)

8.4 Why bother with functions?

Four reasons, in increasing order of importance.

  1. A name. area(3, 4) says what it means. 3 * 4 does not.
  2. No repetition. Write it once, call it many times. Fix a bug in one place.
  3. Smaller pieces. You can check one function is right without holding the whole program in your head.
  4. Reuse. A function that works can be used in the next program too.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Exercise 37

Return the largest of three

Write largest(a, b, c), returning the biggest of the three numbers.

You do not have to compare them yourself. Python has a built-in function called max that does it for you. Hand it some values and it gives back the largest one:

You write You get
max(3, 9) 9
max(3, 9, 4) 9
max(-5, -1, -8) -1

It takes as many values as you like — two, three, or more. min works exactly the same way and gives back the smallest: min(3, 9, 4) is 3.

Note what max does not do. It does not print anything, and it does not change a, b or c. It returns a value, so it has to go somewhere — straight into a return, or into a name:

biggest = max(3, 9, 4)      # biggest is now 9

Your function has the three numbers as parameters. Give all three to max, and return what comes back.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

The whole function body is one line: return max(a, b, c).

Show a worked solution
def largest(a, b, c):
    return max(a, b, c)

print(largest(3, 9, 4))
print(largest(-5, -1, -8))

← Three kinds of error8 of 13Making decisions →

24 minMaking decisions

Every program so far has done the same thing every time. This lesson lets a program choose.

9.1 Comparisons produce True or False

Definition. A Boolean value is either True or False. They are values like any other, and you can store them in variables.

Six operators compare two values and produce a Boolean.

Operator Question
== are they equal?
!= are they different?
< > less than, greater than
<= >= less than or equal, greater than or equal

== compares. = assigns. Confusing the two is one of the most common beginner mistakes, and Python will not let it pass — if x = 5: is a syntax error.

9.2 if

mark = 62

if mark >= 50:
    print("Pass")

The structure is the one you already know from functions: a header line ending in a colon, then an indented block. The block runs only when the condition is True.

else gives the alternative:

if mark >= 50:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")

The pass mark for this module is 50, so >= is the right operator. A mark of exactly 50 passes. > would fail those students, which is the kind of off-by-one that ends up in an appeals meeting.

Exercise 43

Pass or fail

Write result(mark), returning the string "Pass" when the mark is 50 or more, and "Fail" otherwise.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

if mark >= 50: then return "Pass", and else: then return "Fail".

If you used > rather than >=, a mark of exactly 50 fails. Check the second test.

Show a worked solution
def result(mark):
    if mark >= 50:
        return "Pass"
    else:
        return "Fail"

print(result(62))
print(result(50))
print(result(49))

`return` makes `else` optional

return leaves the function immediately, so this is the same function:

def result(mark):
    if mark >= 50:
        return "Pass"
    return "Fail"

If the mark is 50 or more the function returns and the last line never runs. If it is not, the if block is skipped and the last line runs.

Both versions are correct. The shorter one is more common in real Python, and it stays readable when there are several cases.

9.3 elif

For more than two cases, elif — short for “else if” — chains the tests.

if mark >= 70:
    grade = "Distinction"
elif mark >= 60:
    grade = "Merit"
elif mark >= 50:
    grade = "Pass"
else:
    grade = "Fail"

Python takes the first branch that is true and skips all the rest. That is why the order matters: a mark of 75 is greater than 50, but it never reaches that test because the first one already matched.

    grade = "Pass"
elif mark >= 60:
    grade = "Merit"
elif mark >= 70:
    grade = "Distinction"
else:
    grade = "Fail"

print(grade)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

9.4 Combining conditions

and, or and not join Boolean values.

True when
a and b both are true
a or b at least one is true
not a a is false

Python also allows the form you would write in mathematics:

which means exactly mark >= 50 and mark < 70. Most languages do not allow this; Python does, and it reads better.

An `if` that returns True or False is usually unnecessary

Beginners very often write this:

if mark >= 50:
    return True
else:
    return False

The condition mark >= 50 is already True or False. The whole block means the same as:

return mark >= 50

Whenever you find yourself returning True in one branch and False in the other, delete the if and return the condition.

    if year % 100 == 0:

    elif age > 65:

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

age >= 16 is true for a 70-year-old, so Python stops there. Test the narrower condition first.

Show a worked solution
def price(age):
    if age < 16:
        return 5
    elif age > 65:
        return 6
    else:
        return 8

print(price(10), price(30), price(70))

Rule. With elif, test the most specific case first. A broad condition placed early makes every condition after it unreachable — and Python will not warn you, because there is nothing wrong with the code.

← Functions9 of 13Repetition →

34 minRepetition

10.1 The for loop

A loop runs the same block of code several times.

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

prints

0
1
2

The structure is the same shape as a function: a header ending in a colon, then an indented body. The body runs once for each value.

i is the loop variable. It is assigned a new value each time round.

10.2 range

range produces a sequence of whole numbers. It takes up to three arguments.

Call Produces
range(5) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
range(2, 5) 2, 3, 4
range(0, 10, 2) 0, 2, 4, 6, 8

Rule. range stops before the number you give it. range(5) gives five values, and the last one is 4, not 5.

This one rule causes more beginner errors than any other feature of Python. It is worth saying to yourself every time you write range.

Question 17 · predict the output

How many lines, and which numbers?

for i in range(1, 5):
    print(i)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

10.3 Accumulating a result

The commonest use of a loop is building up a value. The pattern has three parts, and it is always the same three:

  1. set a variable before the loop
  2. update it inside the loop
  3. use it after the loop
total = 0                  # before
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i             # inside
print(total)               # after

If you set total = 0 inside the loop, it resets every time round and you get the wrong answer. If you never set it at all, the first total += i fails with a NameError.

10.4 Repetition inside a function

Loops and functions combine. This function draws a line of any character, any number of times.

def line(char, count):
    for i in range(count):
        print(char, end="")
    print()

The end="" stops print moving to a new line, so the characters appear side by side. The final bare print() ends the line once the loop is finished.

10.6 Leaving a loop early

Two keywords change what a loop does part-way through.

Keyword Effect
break leave the loop immediately
continue skip the rest of this turn, go to the next value

break is how you search. Once you have found what you are looking for, there is no reason to keep going.

for n in range(1, 1000):
    if n * n > 500:
        print(n)
        break

That stops at 23. Without the break it would test all 999 numbers and print every one of them.

10.7 A loop inside a loop

The body of a loop can contain another loop. The inner one runs all the way through for every turn of the outer one.

for row in range(1, 4):
    for column in range(1, 4):
        print(row * column, end=" ")
    print()

prints a small multiplication table. The outer loop runs 3 times, the inner one runs 3 times for each of those, so the body runs 9 times in total.

That multiplication is the thing to watch. Two nested loops over a thousand items each is a million steps. This is exactly the cost that made the .count() version of word counting so slow, which you will meet in Session 2.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

After the inner loop finishes, a bare print() ends the row.

Show a worked solution

    for column in range(1, 5):
        print(f"{row * column:>4}", end="")
    print()

The loop variable after the loop

A loop variable still exists after its loop finishes, holding the last value it took:

for i in range(3):
    pass
print(i)        # prints 2

This is occasionally useful and more often a source of confusion, because a name you thought was private to the loop turns out to be visible outside it. Do not rely on it.

More surprising: if the range is empty, the loop body never runs and the variable is never created at all. for i in range(0): pass followed by print(i) raises a NameError.

← Making decisions10 of 13Local variables and tracebacks →

20 minLocal variables and tracebacks

11.1 Variables inside a function are local

Definition. A variable created inside a function is local to it. It exists while the function runs, and disappears when the function returns.

def add_tax(price):
    tax = price * 0.2
    return price + tax

print(add_tax(100))
print(tax)              # NameError

The last line fails. tax existed only inside add_tax.

This is a feature, not a restriction. It means you can use the name total inside twenty different functions without any of them interfering with each other. You never have to check whether a name is already taken somewhere else in the program.

Parameters are local too. Assigning to a parameter inside a function does not change anything outside it.

Each call gets its own frame: a private set of names. The frame is created when the function is called and thrown away when it returns.

Question 18 · predict the output

Does the function change it?

def rename(label):
    label = "changed"
    return label

original = "kept"
result = rename(original)

print(original)
print(result)

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

11.2 Reading a traceback

When an error happens inside a function, Python shows you the chain of calls that led to it. This is a traceback.

your code, line 3, in add_tax
    return price + tax
your code, line 6, in <module>
    print(add_tax("100"))
TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'

Read it from the bottom up:

  1. The last line names the error and describes it.
  2. Above that is the line that was running when it failed.
  3. Above that is what called it, and so on.

The bottom line tells you what went wrong. The lines above tell you how you got there. Often the real mistake is not in the failing line at all, but in the line that called it with the wrong value.

In the example above, add_tax is fine. The mistake is on line 6, where the argument is the string "100" instead of the number 100.

Exercise 61

Fix a scope error

This program fails with a NameError. The total is calculated inside the function, but used outside it.

Fix it by returning the value and storing it. Do not move the calculation out of the function.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Add return total as the last line of the function.

Then the caller needs to keep the answer: result = add_tax(100).

Show a worked solution
def add_tax(price):
    total = price * 1.2
    return total

result = add_tax(100)
print("Total:", result)

Why not just use a global variable?

Python does allow a function to read a variable defined outside it, and there is a global keyword that lets one write to it.

Almost always, do not. A function that depends on outside variables cannot be understood on its own, cannot be tested on its own, and breaks when anything else in the program changes that variable.

Rule. Pass values in as arguments. Get values out with return. A function whose behaviour depends only on its arguments is one you can trust.

11.3 Practice

Exercise 62

Pass values in, return values out

report currently reads width and height from outside itself. That works, but only by accident: the function cannot be used with any other rectangle, and it breaks the moment those names change.

Rewrite it to take width and height as parameters and return the string.

report(3, 4) must return "3 x 4 = 12".

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Move width and height into the brackets of the def line.

The caller now supplies the numbers: print(report(3, 4)).

Show a worked solution
def report(width, height):
    return f"{width} x {height} = {width * height}"

print(report(3, 4))

Exercise 63

Use a traceback to find the caller’s mistake

safe_divide is correct. The call is wrong: it passes a string where a number is needed.

Run it and read the traceback. It names two lines. The one to fix is the call, not the function.

Correct the call so the program prints 5.0.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

The traceback’s bottom line says a string and an integer cannot be divided.

Show a worked solution

answer = safe_divide(10, 2)

← Repetition11 of 13Recursion →

23 minRecursion

A function can call itself. That sounds like a trick or a mistake, and it is neither — it is the natural way to write anything whose definition refers to a smaller version of itself.

12.1 Why it works

The last lesson is the whole explanation. Every call gets its own frame, with its own copies of the parameters and local variables. A function calling itself is just another call, and it gets another frame. The two frames do not interfere, because no frame can see inside another.

So countdown(3) can call countdown(2) without either one confusing the other’s n.

12.2 Two parts, always

Definition. A recursive function calls itself. Every recursive function needs two things:

  1. a base case — a value it can answer immediately, without calling itself
  2. a recursive case — which calls itself with input that is closer to the base case

Miss the base case and it never stops. Fail to get closer to it and it never stops either.

def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:            # base case
        print("Go!")
    else:                 # recursive case
        print(n)
        countdown(n - 1)  # closer to 0 every time

countdown(3) prints 3, then calls countdown(2), which prints 2, and so on until countdown(0) prints Go! and returns without calling anything.

Exercise 64

Count down, without a loop

Write countdown(n) using recursion. It prints every number from n down to 1, then prints Go!. No for and no while.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

The base case is n == 0: print Go! and stop.

Otherwise print n, then call countdown(n - 1).

Show a worked solution
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Go!")
    else:
        print(n)
        countdown(n - 1)

countdown(3)

12.3 Returning a value

Printing is the easy case. Returning is where recursion earns its keep.

The factorial of n is n × (n−1) × … × 1, and its definition is already recursive: factorial(n) is n * factorial(n - 1), with factorial(0) defined as 1.

That definition is the code.

Exercise 65

Factorial

Write factorial(n). factorial(0) is 1; otherwise it is n * factorial(n - 1).

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

if n == 0: return 1 is the base case.

The recursive case is a single line: return n * factorial(n - 1).

Show a worked solution
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

print(factorial(0))
print(factorial(5))

Why `factorial(0)` is 1

It looks arbitrary, but it is forced. factorial(1) must be 1 * factorial(0), and factorial(1) is 1, so factorial(0) must be 1.

Choosing the base case well is most of the work in a recursive function. A base case of n == 1 would also work here, but then factorial(0) would recurse forever into negative numbers — the base case would be unreachable from below.

Rule. Ask what the smallest sensible input is, and make sure your base case catches it.

12.4 When it goes wrong

A recursion that never reaches its base case does not run forever. Python gives up.

Each call needs a frame, and frames use memory, so Python limits how deep it will go — about a thousand calls. Past that it raises RecursionError.

That limit is a feature. It turns a bug that would exhaust your machine’s memory into an ordinary error message that names the problem.

Question 20 · predict the output

What stops this?

def forever(n):
    return forever(n - 1)

print(forever(5))

If you think it stops with an error, write the word error on that line. You do not have to reproduce the message.

Exercise 66

Give it a base case

total(n) should add up every whole number from n down to 1, so total(4) is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1, which is 10.

As written it has no base case and raises RecursionError. Add one.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Run it first and read the error. RecursionError almost always means a missing or unreachable base case.

What should total(0) be? Adding up no numbers gives 0. Return that.

Show a worked solution
def total(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return n + total(n - 1)

print(total(4))

12.5 Recursion or a loop?

Anything you can write with recursion you can write with a loop, and the other way round. So which?

Loop Recursion
Memory one frame one frame per level
Depth limit none about 1000 in Python
Speed in Python faster slower
Reads well when you are repeating a step the problem is defined in terms of itself

For counting and totalling, use a loop — that is what loops are for, and Python loops are faster than Python function calls.

Recursion earns its place when the structure of the data is recursive: a folder that contains folders, a family tree, an expression with brackets inside brackets. You will meet those in Session 2 and Session 3. Writing them with loops is possible and unpleasant.

12.6 Practice

Exercise 67

Raise to a power

Write power(base, exponent) recursively. power(2, 10) is 1024.

Anything to the power 0 is 1 — that is your base case. Otherwise base ** n is base * base ** (n - 1).

Do not use ** or pow.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

if exponent == 0: return 1.

return base * power(base, exponent - 1).

Show a worked solution
def power(base, exponent):
    if exponent == 0:
        return 1
    return base * power(base, exponent - 1)

print(power(2, 10))
print(power(5, 0))

Exercise 68 · check the AI's answer

An AI model wrote this. It never finishes.

An assistant was asked for “a recursive function that counts the digits in a whole number”.

The idea is right: digits(n) is 1 plus the number of digits in n // 10. But there is no base case, so it recurses past zero into negative numbers until Python stops it.

Add a base case. A number below 10 has exactly one digit.

Written by an AI model · a general-purpose coding assistant · 2026-08-21

def digits(n):
    return 1 + digits(n // 10)

print(digits(8165))

Nobody has checked this. That is your job.

Ctrl/Cmd + Enter to run · Esc to leave the editor

Run it first. RecursionError is what a missing base case looks like.

if n < 10: return 1. Note that this also handles 0 correctly.

Show a worked solution
def digits(n):
    if n < 10:
        return 1
    return 1 + digits(n // 10)

print(digits(8165))

Rule. When you write a recursive function, write the base case first. It is the part that makes it stop, and it is the part generated code most often leaves out.

5 minWhat you learned

13.1 Summary

Python is interpreted. It translates and runs your code line by line. There is no separate build step, and an error appears only when Python reaches that line.

Every value has a type. 42, 42.0 and "42" are three different things. Python will not convert between them without being asked.

A name is attached to a value by assignment. Assigning again moves the name. Read a program from the top to know what a name holds.

Three kinds of error. A syntax error stops everything before it starts. A runtime error stops at one line, after the earlier lines have run. A semantic error does not stop anything, and is the dangerous one.

A function takes arguments and returns a value. Its local variables belong to it alone. print shows a value; return gives it back.

if chooses; elif chains. Python takes the first branch that is true and skips the rest, so the most specific test must come first.

range stops before its upper limit. range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4.

A recursive function needs a base case. Write it first — it is the part that makes the function stop, and the part most often left out.

13.2 What the machine got wrong today

Five times today you were handed code that ran, looked correct, and was not.

Where The mistake How you found it
temperature brackets in the wrong place checked a value you knew
averages printed instead of returning the result was None
ticket prices a broad elif before a narrow one tested a case in each band
numbered list range stopped one line early counted the lines
counting digits no base case it raised RecursionError

And once, in the lesson on arithmetic, Python itself was the surprise: round(2.5) is 2, not 3. No assistant was involved. That one is worth remembering separately, because it is the kind of thing an assistant will get wrong for you later.

None of those needed expert knowledge. Each needed one habit: decide what the answer should be, then check.

13.3 Optional practice

Not homework. Do it if you want more.

  1. Write bottles(n), printing the “99 bottles of beer” verses from n down to 1. Use an if for the last verse, where the word is singular.
  2. Write fizzbuzz(n), printing the numbers 1 to n, but Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5, and FizzBuzz for both. The order of your tests decides whether it works.
  3. Write fibonacci(n) recursively: 0, 1, and after that each number is the sum of the two before it. Then try fibonacci(35) and notice how long it takes. Ask yourself how many times it recalculates fibonacci(10).
  4. Break something on purpose. Take a working exercise, introduce one mistake, and decide which of the three kinds of error it is before you run it.
  5. Ask an assistant for a function you already wrote today. Compare its version with yours. Where they differ, work out which is right, and why.

13.4 The numbers you used today

Every figure in the practice exercises is real, and all of it is within a short walk or Metro ride of the campus.

Where What you used Read more
Grey’s Monument 41 m tall, 164 steps, finished 1838 Grey’s Monument
High Level Bridge opened 1849, Robert Stephenson, rail above road High Level Bridge
Stephenson’s Rocket built 1829 on Forth Street; 12 mph average, 30 mph top Rocket · Railway Museum
Tyne Bridge opened 1928, 161.8 m span, 26 m above the water Tyne Bridge
Millennium Bridge opened 2001, 850 tonnes, 40° in about four minutes Millennium Bridge
St James’ Park 52,719 seats, 19 home league matches St James’ Park
The Castle Keep 1080 castle, 1172–1177 stone keep, £1,144 The Castle
Tyne and Wear Metro opened 1980, 60 stations, 77.5 km Metro
Joseph Swan electric lamp shown 1879; Lit & Phil lit 1880 Joseph Swan
Turbinia launched 1894, 34.5 knots, Spithead 1897 Turbinia
Angel of the North 1998, 20 m tall, 54 m wingspan, 208 tonnes Angel of the North
Great North Run 13.1 miles, started 1981, largest in the world Great North Run

Why this city, for engineers

Four of those are not local curiosities. They changed how the world works, and they happened within a few miles of each other.

George and Robert Stephenson made the railway locomotive practical. Rocket was built on Forth Street, a mile from here, in 1829. Robert went on to build railways on four continents, and designed the High Level Bridge you can walk across this afternoon.

Joseph Swan made the first practical incandescent light bulb and demonstrated it on Westgate Road in 1879. He patented the carbon filament in 1880, and his company later merged with Edison’s.

William Armstrong built hydraulic machinery that opened bridges and dock gates around the world, and lit Cragside — the first house anywhere lit by electricity generated from water — using Swan’s lamps.

Charles Parsons invented the steam turbine and proved it with Turbinia on the Tyne. Most of the world’s electricity is still generated by turbines descended from his.

Charles Grey, whose column stands at the top of Grey Street, was also the Prime Minister who carried the Great Reform Act of 1832.

You are studying engineering in a city that has form. Go and look at the bridges — and at Turbinia, which is ten minutes away in the Discovery Museum and free to visit.

Today’s material is roughly its chapters 1 to 3. If any of it went past too quickly, that is the place to go over it again at your own pace.
